svg.title: Front view muscle chart. Primary muscles: Lats, Upper Back. Secondary muscles: Traps, Lower Back, Rear Delts, Biceps.
Back view muscle chart. Primary muscles: Lats, Upper Back. Secondary muscles: Traps, Lower Back, Rear Delts, Biceps.

svg.text: Bar at the knees, back flat
It takes the lats from a full overhead stretch to a full contraction against your whole bodyweight, and nothing
else here moves that much lat range with nothing to lean on.
Standing up as the bar comes in — the hinge angle disappears and the legs and lower back finish a rep the lats were
Rowing to the sternum with flared elbows — it becomes a rear-delt raise and drags the shoulder blades out of
Letting the lower back round to reach the floor between reps — a loaded, flexed spine is the single riskiest
Hinge at the hips to about 45°, back flat, bar hanging at the knees. Row
the bar to your lower ribs, squeezing the shoulder blades. Lower under
control without standing up or jerking.
Breathing — Inhale and brace at the hang, exhale as you row the bar into your
lower ribs, then breathe in again as you lower it under control.
Coach's cue — Lead with the elbows and keep the neck neutral — no chin tucking
Hinge only as far as you can hold a flat back — about 45° is plenty; if
your hamstrings cannot hold that position, use a chest-supported row
Keep the load light enough that the torso does not bounce, and choose a
supported row if you have a current lumbar injury or you are rowing

Best on paper is not always best for you. Which exercise builds a body part fastest depends on your build, your injury history and how much of the movement you already own — someone who cannot yet hold

a flat back under load will get more from the exercise ranked third than from the one ranked first. Treat this as a starting point for a conversation, not a verdict: ask a coach on the floor before you
